games.title: Review — Skin, Embryology, Spine & Skull: quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 1 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which cell type located in the stratum basale of the epidermis functions primarily as a mechanoreceptor for light touch?
questions.explanation: Merkel cells reside in the stratum basale and pair with nerve endings to serve as mechanoreceptors for light touch sensation.

questions.q: Which embryonic mesodermal derivative directly gives rise to the vertebrae and ribs?
questions.explanation: The sclerotome, formed from the medial part of somites, gives rise to the vertebral column and ribs.

questions.q: Failure of the caudal neuropore to close near the end of the fourth week of embryonic development results in which congenital defect?
questions.explanation: Failure of the caudal neuropore to close leads to neural tube defects affecting the spine, most commonly spina bifida.

questions.q: Which anatomical feature is unique to cervical vertebrae compared to thoracic and lumbar vertebrae?
questions.explanation: Transverse foramina are exclusive to cervical vertebrae and transmit the vertebral arteries and veins (except through C7).

questions.q: Which ligament connects the tips of the spinous processes from the C7 vertebra down to the sacrum?
questions.explanation: The supraspinous ligament runs along the tips of the spinous processes from C7 to the sacrum, merging superiorly with the nuchal ligament.

questions.q: Which structure passes through the foramen spinosum of the sphenoid bone to enter the cranial cavity?
questions.explanation: The foramen spinosum allows passage of the middle meningeal artery and the meningeal branch of the mandibular nerve into the middle cranial fossa.

questions.q: The junction where the sagittal, coronal, and frontal sutures intersect on the fetal skull forms which structure?
questions.explanation: The anterior fontanelle is located at the intersection of the coronal, sagittal, and frontal sutures, eventually closing to form the bregma.

questions.q: Meckel's cartilage, which provides a template for the development of the mandible and forms the malleus and incus, arises from which pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation: Meckel's cartilage develops within the first pharyngeal arch (mandibular arch) and contributes to the ossicles of the middle ear and lower jaw development.

questions.q: Which type of skin gland secretes a viscous, protein- and lipid-rich sweat into hair follicles in response to stress and hormonal stimulation starting at puberty?
questions.explanation: Apocrine sweat glands are concentrated in axillary and anogenital regions and produce a viscous secretion starting at puberty.

questions.q: At which vertebral level does the spinal cord typically terminate as the conus medullaris in a healthy adult?
questions.explanation: In adults, the spinal cord tapers off as the conus medullaris at the L1–L2 vertebral level.

games.title: Micronutrients: quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which of the following is the hallmark ocular manifestation of severe Vitamin A deficiency in children?
questions.explanation: Bitot spots are dry, silvery-grey triangular patches of keratinized conjunctiva pathognomonic of Vitamin A deficiency.

questions.q: A 12-month-old exclusively breastfed infant presents with severe pallor, irritability, and developmental stagnation. Dietary history reveals no supplementation. Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.explanation: Infants exclusively breastfed by vegan mothers are at high risk of Vitamin B12 deficiency, presenting with megaloblastic anemia and neurological regression.

questions.q: What is the recommended daily oral elemental iron supplementation dose for the treatment of iron deficiency anemia in children?
questions.explanation: The therapeutic dose of elemental iron for children with iron deficiency anemia is 3 to 6 mg/kg/day divided into 1-3 doses.

questions.q: Which clinical finding is most characteristic of infantile scurvy resulting from Vitamin C deficiency?
options: Pseudoparalysis due to subperiosteal bone hemorrhages
questions.explanation: Scurvy in infants typically presents with painful extremities leading to a 'frog-leg' position and pseudoparalysis caused by subperiosteal hemorrhages.

questions.q: A toddler presents with growth retardation, delayed wound healing, alopecia, and a periorificial pustular rash. What is the most likely micronutrient deficiency?
questions.explanation: Acrodermatitis enteropathica, characterized by periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhea, is classic for zinc deficiency.

questions.q: Which of the following radiological features is classically seen in the wrist radiographs of an infant with active rickets?
questions.explanation: Active nutritional rickets leads to widened, cupped, and frayed metaphyses along with widening of the epiphyseal plate due to unmineralized osteoid.

questions.q: Wernicke encephalopathy in children, caused by thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency, classically presents with which constellation of symptoms?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of Wernicke encephalopathy comprises ocular abnormalities, ataxia, and altered mental status.

questions.q: In acute watery diarrhea in children living in developing countries, supplementation with which micronutrient has been shown to reduce the duration and severity of the episode?
questions.explanation: WHO guidelines recommend 10-14 days of zinc supplementation during acute diarrhea to shorten duration and reduce recurrence.

questions.q: Which vitamin deficiency leads to impaired carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, predisposing neonates to hemorrhagic disease?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is an essential cofactor for the gamma-glutamyl carboxylase that activates coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X.

questions.q: A child with chronic fat malabsorption due to cystic fibrosis presents with hemolytic anemia, posterior column spinal cord degeneration, and ataxia. This is due to a deficiency in:
questions.explanation: Vitamin E deficiency causes a neurologic syndrome resembling Friedreich ataxia and hemolytic anemia due to increased erythrocyte fragility.

games.title: Gastritis: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 65-year-old female presents with epigastric distress, nausea, and dark stools for 2 days. She has a history of severe osteoarthritis and has been taking high-dose daily ibuprofen for the past 3 weeks. Upper endoscopy reveals multiple superficial mucosal erosions with petechiae in the gastric antrum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Heavy NSAID use directly inhibits mucosal prostaglandin synthesis, disrupting the mucosal protective barrier and leading to acute erosive gastritis.

questions.q: A 42-year-old male presents with a 4-month history of burning epigastric pain that worsens a few hours after meals and improves with antacids. He reports no weight loss, dysphagia, or hematemesis, and his physical examination is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori
questions.explanation: In patients under 55-60 years of age with uninvestigated dyspepsia and no alarm symptoms, a non-invasive 'test-and-treat' strategy for H. pylori, such as a urea breath test, is recommended.

questions.q: A 58-year-old female presents with progressive fatigue, numbness in her lower extremities, and a smooth, shiny red tongue. Laboratory testing reveals macrocytic anemia and markedly low serum vitamin B12 levels. Gastric mucosal biopsy shows diffuse mucosal atrophy primarily restricted to the fundus and body. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Autoimmune metaplastic atrophic gastritis targets parietal cells located in the gastric body and fundus, resulting in intrinsic factor deficiency and subsequent pernicious anemia.

questions.q: A 48-year-old male is admitted to the intensive care unit following severe thermal burns covering 40% of his total body surface area. On day 4 of hospitalization, he develops coffee-ground emesis and melena. Endoscopy reveals extensive diffuse superficial mucosal lesions throughout the stomach. What is the primary underlying mechanism responsible for this patient's gastric pathology?
options: Direct bacterial invasion of the gastric muscularis
Hypergastrinemia due to a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor
questions.explanation: Stress-induced mucosal disease (such as a Curling ulcer in burn victims) develops primarily due to splanchnic hypoperfusion and ischemia, which severely compromises mucosal defenses.

questions.q: A 52-year-old male presents with persistent epigastric discomfort and early satiety over 3 months. Gastric biopsy reveals chronic active gastritis associated with H. pylori and dense lymphocytic infiltrates consistent with low-grade mucosal-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma. What is the most appropriate initial management step?
questions.explanation: Eradication of Helicobacter pylori using antibiotic and proton pump inhibitor therapy leads to complete tumor regression in the majority of early-stage, low-grade gastric MALT lymphomas.

questions.q: A 29-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a night of heavy alcohol binge drinking with acute epigastric pain and several episodes of emesis with blood streaks. Vital signs are stable and abdominal examination shows mild, non-rebound epigastric tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Direct toxic mucosal injury from acute heavy alcohol ingestion commonly causes acute hemorrhagic gastropathy, presenting with epigastric pain and minor upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents with chronic epigastric pain, weight loss, and bilateral lower extremity pitting edema. Endoscopy demonstrates giant, tortuous gastric rugal folds predominantly affecting the gastric body, and laboratory testing reveals significant hypoalbuminemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Menetrier disease is a rare hypertrophic gastropathy characterized by massive enlargement of gastric rugal folds and severe enteric protein loss leading to hypoalbuminemia.

questions.q: A 62-year-old immunocompromised female presents with acute severe epigastric pain, high fever, chills, and purulent vomiting. Physical examination reveals generalized abdominal rigidity, and emergency surgery shows purulent inflammation infiltrating the submucosa of the gastric wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Phlegmonous gastritis is a rare, life-threatening bacterial infection of the gastric submucosa and muscularis, presenting with acute severe abdominal pain, sepsis, and purulent emesis.

games.title: Bleeding Disorders: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with petechiae on her extremities and mucosal bleeding from her gums for 3 days. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 12,000/µL, normal hemoglobin, and normal WBC count. Peripheral blood smear shows sparse, large platelets without schistocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Isolated thrombocytopenia with normal coagulation studies and an absence of schistocytes on blood smear in an otherwise healthy young female is characteristic of immune thrombocytopenia (ITP).

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic due to painful swelling in his right knee after a minor fall. Coagulation profile reveals a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) that corrects with a 1:1 mix of normal plasma, while prothrombin time (PT) and bleeding time are normal. Deficiency of which factor is the most likely cause of this presentation?
questions.explanation: An isolated prolonged aPTT that corrects with a 1:1 mixing study in a young male presenting with hemarthrosis strongly points to Factor VIII deficiency (Hemophilia A).

questions.q: A 23-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding and frequent epistaxis since menarche. Laboratory testing reveals a normal platelet count, normal PT, slightly prolonged aPTT, and significantly reduced ristocetin cofactor activity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Mucocutaneous bleeding accompanied by a prolonged aPTT and decreased ristocetin cofactor activity is diagnostic of von Willebrand disease.

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with confusion, fever, petechiae, and dark urine. Laboratory testing demonstrates a hemoglobin of 7.5 g/dL, platelet count of 18,000/µL, elevated LDH, and multiple schistocytes on peripheral blood smear. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation: Suspected thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) requires immediate therapeutic plasma exchange to reduce high mortality rates.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man in the ICU for Escherichia coli sepsis develops oozing from peripheral IV sites and skin ecchymoses. Laboratory testing reveals prolonged PT and aPTT, decreased fibrinogen, elevated D-dimer, and a platelet count of 35,000/µL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sepsis-induced systemic activation of coagulation leading to prolonged PT/aPTT, consumption of platelets and fibrinogen, and elevated D-dimer confirms disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

questions.q: A 72-year-old man on prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy following abdominal surgery presents with new skin ecchymoses and oozing from venipuncture sites. Laboratory studies show a PT of 24 seconds (INR 2.5) and an aPTT of 38 seconds, with a platelet count of 220,000/µL. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Eradication of gut flora by broad-spectrum antibiotics reduces Vitamin K production, leading to prolongation of Vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (elevated PT/INR) which rapidly responds to Vitamin K administration.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man being treated with unfractionated heparin for a deep vein thrombosis experiences a 50% drop in platelet count on day 6 of therapy. Ultrasound reveals extension of the deep vein thrombus, but he has no active bleeding. What is the immediate next step in management?
options: Switch from unfractionated heparin to low-molecular-weight heparin
Continue heparin and monitor platelet counts daily
questions.explanation: Suspected Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) requires immediate discontinuation of all heparin formulations and initiation of a non-heparin anticoagulant like argatroban to reduce thrombotic risk.

questions.q: A newborn boy presents with delayed umbilical cord bleeding and recurrent subcutaneous hematomas. Coagulation screen shows normal PT, normal aPTT, normal thrombin time, and normal platelet count, but clot solubility in 5M urea is abnormal. What is the most likely underlying bleeding disorder?
questions.explanation: Normal routine coagulation studies (PT, aPTT, TT) with abnormal clot dissolution in 5M urea is pathognomonic for Factor XIII deficiency.

games.title: Scleroderma: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which class of medication is the first-line treatment for managing a scleroderma renal crisis?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors, such as captopril, are the drug of choice for treating scleroderma renal crisis as they significantly reduce mortality and help restore renal function.

questions.q: Which medication class is associated with an increased risk of precipitating a scleroderma renal crisis and should be used with caution in systemic sclerosis?
questions.explanation: Moderate-to-high doses of corticosteroids (e.g., prednisolone >15 mg/day) are a well-documented risk factor for triggering scleroderma renal crisis.

questions.q: What is the first-line pharmacological agent used to manage Raynaud's phenomenon in patients with systemic sclerosis?
questions.explanation: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, particularly oral nifedipine, are recommended as the first-line pharmacological treatment for Raynaud's phenomenon.

questions.q: Bosentan is used in systemic sclerosis to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension and prevent digital ulcers. What is its primary mechanism of action?
options: Direct stimulation of soluble guanylate cyclase
questions.explanation: Bosentan is a dual endothelin receptor antagonist (inhibiting ET-A and ET-B receptors) that blocks endothelin-1-mediated vasoconstriction and vascular proliferation.

questions.q: Nintedanib is approved to slow the decline of pulmonary function in systemic sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease (SSc-ILD). What is its mechanism of action?
questions.explanation: Nintedanib is an oral small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor that targets VEGFR, FGFR, and PDGFR to inhibit pathways involved in pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.q: Mycophenolate mofetil is frequently used for skin and lung manifestations of systemic sclerosis. Which enzyme does its active metabolite selectively inhibit?
questions.explanation: Mycophenolic acid selectively and reversibly inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH), suppressing de novo purine synthesis required for T and B lymphocyte proliferation.

questions.q: A patient with systemic sclerosis presents with severe digital ischemia refractory to oral vasodilators. Which intravenous medication is indicated for severe Raynaud's phenomenon and digital ulcer healing?
questions.explanation: Intravenous iloprost, a synthetic prostacyclin analogue, provides potent vasodilation and anti-platelet effects for severe or refractory Raynaud's phenomenon and digital ischemia.

questions.q: Sildenafil is used to manage severe Raynaud's phenomenon and pulmonary hypertension in systemic sclerosis. What is its mechanism of action?
questions.explanation: Sildenafil selectively inhibits phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5), preventing cyclic GMP degradation and leading to vascular smooth muscle relaxation.

games.title: Pulmonary tuberculosis: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child being treated for pulmonary tuberculosis presents with tingling sensations and numbness in their feet. Which first-line anti-tuberculosis medication is most commonly associated with this adverse effect?
questions.explanation: Isoniazid can cause peripheral neuropathy due to interference with pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) metabolism.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child with pulmonary tuberculosis starts anti-tuberculosis therapy. The parents are anxious because the child's urine and tears have turned an orange-red color. Which drug is responsible for this harmless side effect?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin characteristically causes a harmless orange-red discoloration of body fluids including urine, tears, and sweat.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of Rifampicin in the treatment of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infections?
options: Inhibition of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
Disruption of bacterial cell membrane potential
questions.explanation: Rifampicin acts by inhibiting bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, thereby suppressing bacterial RNA synthesis.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child on treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis reports blurred vision and difficulty distinguishing between red and green colors. Which drug is the most likely cause of these visual symptoms?
questions.explanation: Ethambutol causes optic neuritis, which typically manifests as decreased visual acuity and loss of red-green color discrimination.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child with severe pulmonary tuberculosis is prescribed isoniazid. To prevent isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy, which supplement should be co-prescribed?
questions.explanation: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) supplementation is co-administered with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy, particularly in high-risk or malnourished children.

questions.q: What is the mechanism of action of Isoniazid in pediatric tuberculosis management?
options: Inhibits synthesis of mycolic acids essential for the bacterial cell wall
Binds to 30S ribosomal subunit to block protein synthesis
questions.explanation: Isoniazid is a prodrug that inhibits the synthesis of mycolic acids, which are essential components of the mycobacterial cell wall.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child treated for drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis develops elevated serum uric acid levels. Which anti-tuberculosis medication is most frequently associated with hyperuricemia?
questions.explanation: Pyrazinamide inhibits the renal excretion of uric acid, frequently leading to hyperuricemia.

questions.q: Which anti-tuberculosis medication works by inhibiting arabinosyl transferase, an enzyme critical for mycobacterial cell wall synthesis?
questions.explanation: Ethambutol exerts its bacteriostatic effect by inhibiting arabinosyl transferase, thereby impairing arabinogalactan synthesis in the mycobacterial cell wall.
